title: Core Academics
description: Mathematics, reading and writing, science (physics, chemistry, biology and the human body), geography, history and economics basics, taught through everyday life at home.

nodes.title: Shapes and patterns

nodes.title: Adding and taking away

nodes.title: Measuring and estimating

nodes.title: Algebra
nodes.description: Use letters for unknown numbers and solve simple equations.

nodes.title: Functions and graphs

nodes.title: Applied mathematics

nodes.title: Reading stories

nodes.title: Understanding texts

nodes.description: Write a clear paragraph with a main idea and details.

nodes.title: Essays and reports
nodes.description: Plan and write structured essays and lab reports.

nodes.title: Observing
nodes.description: Look closely, describe and ask what will happen.

nodes.title: Materials
nodes.description: Sort materials by what they are like: hard, soft, floats, sinks.

nodes.title: Fair tests
nodes.description: Change one thing at a time and record results.

nodes.title: Forces and motion
nodes.description: Pushes, pulls, friction and gravity.

nodes.title: Chemical changes
nodes.description: Acids, bases and reactions you can see at home.

nodes.title: Energy and electricity

nodes.title: Scientific method

nodes.title: Body parts

competencies.title: Can read a short book alone
Can use fractions to scale a recipe
Can explain how the main body systems work together
Can write a science lab report

items.subject: mathematics
items.title: Count the toys
items.summary: Let us count toys, one by one!
steps: Put five toys in a row.
Touch each toy and say a number: one, two, three...
How many toys? Say the last number again.
Add one more toy. Count again!

check.question: You count 1, 2, 3. How many toys are there?
check.explain: Yes! The last number you say tells how many.

check.question: You add one more to 3 toys. Now there are...
check.explain: One more than 3 is 4. Well done!

items.adultNote: Any small objects work: spoons, stones, pegs. Use items too big to swallow. Let the child touch each one as they count.

items.subject: mathematics
items.title: Shape hunt
items.summary: Find circles, squares and triangles at home.
steps: Look at a plate. It is a circle!
Find a square. Maybe a window or a cushion?
Find a triangle. Look at a slice of bread cut corner to corner.
Draw one shape in the air with your finger.

check.question: A plate is round. What shape is it?
check.explain: Yes, a plate is a circle.

check.question: How many sides does a triangle have?
check.explain: A triangle has 3 sides. Count them with your finger!

items.adultNote: Name shapes as you see them during the day. Corners and sides are good words to introduce.

items.subject: biology
items.title: My body parts
items.summary: Eyes see. Ears hear. My heart goes thump!
steps: Touch your head.
Point to your eyes, ears, nose and mouth.
What do eyes do? They see!
Put a hand on your chest. Your heart pumps and your lungs breathe.
Squeeze your arm. Bones are hard inside. Muscles help you move.

check.question: What do we use to hear?
check.explain: Yes! Ears help us hear.

check.question: What pumps inside your chest?
check.explain: Your heart pumps blood all day and night.

check.question: What is hard inside your arm?
check.explain: Bones are hard. They hold you up.

items.adultNote: Covers brief section 6 level 1: head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, heart, lungs, stomach, bones, muscles, skin. Sing a "touch your..." song to make it a game.

items.subject: reading
items.title: Sound of the day
items.summary: Every letter makes a sound. Let us find one!
steps: Adult says a sound, like "mmm".
Say it together: mmm.
Find things that start with mmm: mum, milk, moon.
Draw the letter in the air, then in sand or on paper.

check.question: Which word starts with "mmm"?
check.explain: Moon starts with mmm. Great listening!

check.question: Which word starts with "sss"?
check.explain: Sock starts with sss, like a snake.

items.adultNote: Say the letter sound (mmm), not the letter name (em). One sound a day is plenty.

items.subject: science
items.title: Sink or float?
items.summary: Will it sink? Will it float? Let us guess and see.
steps: 🥣 An adult helps fill a shallow bowl with water.
🥄 Pick a spoon, a leaf, a cork and a stone.
🤔 Guess: sink or float?
💧 Drop it in gently. Watch!
✅ Was your guess right? Try one more thing.

safety.notes: Water play for young children needs an adult beside them the whole time. Use a shallow bowl, not a bath or bucket, and empty it straight after. Use objects too big to swallow and wipe spills straight away. If an egg is used, wash hands afterwards.

basic.description: Test four things from around the home and sort them into two piles.

better.description: Make a ball of foil, then flatten it into a boat. Does the shape change sink or float?

advanced.description: Add salt to the water and see if an egg that sank now floats. Record results in a table.

substitutions.use: Any bowl, pot or the kitchen sink with a little water

check.question: A stone in water will...
check.explain: Stones are heavy for their size, so they sink.

check.question: A leaf in water will...
check.explain: A leaf is light and flat, so it floats.

sources.title: Accident prevention advice
sources.publisher: Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA)

items.subject: mathematics
items.title: Adding and taking away with fruit
items.summary: Use real fruit (or pictures) to add and take away.
steps: Put 4 pieces of fruit on the table.
Add 3 more. Count them all. 4 + 3 = 7.
Now eat (or move away) 2. How many left? 7 - 2 = 5.
Write each number sentence on paper.
Make up your own for someone else to solve.

check.explain: Count on from 5: 6, 7, 8.

check.question: You have 6 apples and give away 2. How many are left?
check.explain: 6 take away 2 is 4.

check.question: Which is the same as 3 + 4?
check.explain: You can add numbers in any order and get the same answer.

items.subject: mathematics
items.title: Measure a bicycle
items.summary: Guess, then measure a bike wheel, the frame and the handlebars.
steps: Guess how wide the wheel is. Write your guess.
Measure the wheel from edge to edge with a tape or string.
Measure the handlebars and the seat height.
Put a chalk mark on the tyre. Roll the bike one full turn and measure how far it went.
Compare your guesses with the real numbers. Which guess was closest?

hazards: Bike can tip over onto feet
safety.notes: Keep the bike standing still, leaning on a wall or held by a helper. Never put fingers in the spokes or chain. Roll the bike by walking it, not riding it, on flat ground away from traffic.

materials: A stick or ruler marked in hand-spans
basic.description: Measure with string, then lay the string along a ruler or count hand-spans.

better.description: Measure in centimetres and record every measurement in a table.

advanced.description: Measure the distance of one wheel turn, then work out how many turns it takes to travel 100 metres.

substitutions.use: A toy car, pram, scooter or any wheel at home
String plus a ruler, or a sheet of paper (about 30 cm long)

check.question: Why do we guess before we measure?
check.explain: Good estimators can spot when a measurement looks wrong.

check.question: A bigger wheel goes ___ in one turn.
check.explain: A bigger wheel has a longer edge, so it rolls further each turn.

items.adultNote: Pairs well with the bicycle pathway (measurement, forces, gears). Any wheel works if there is no bicycle.

items.subject: biology
items.title: Bones and muscles
items.summary: Your skeleton holds you up. Your muscles pull your bones to move.
steps: Feel the bones in your hand. How many can you find?
Bend your arm. Feel the muscle on top get fat and hard. It is pulling!
Straighten your arm. Now the muscle underneath pulls.
Draw a stick skeleton and label skull, ribs, spine and leg bones.
Talk about it: why does a skeleton need joints?

check.question: What protects your heart and lungs?
check.explain: Your ribs make a strong cage around your heart and lungs.

check.question: Muscles move bones by...
check.explain: Muscles can only pull. That is why they work in pairs.

items.subject: reading
items.title: Read it, retell it
items.summary: Read a short story, then tell it back in your own words.
steps: Choose a short story book or a free online story.
Read it aloud, or take turns with an adult.
Close the book. Tell what happened at the beginning, middle and end.
Who was your favourite character? Why?
Draw one picture of the best part.

check.question: A story usually has a beginning, a middle and...
check.explain: Beginning, middle and end help you remember the story.

check.question: Retelling means...
options: saying the story in your own words
check.explain: Using your own words shows you understood it.

items.adultNote: Public libraries and free legal digital libraries are fine sources. Re-reading favourite books is good practice too.

items.subject: geography
items.title: Map my room
items.summary: Draw your room as a bird sees it from above.
steps: Stand in the doorway and look around.
Draw the shape of the room on paper.
Add the bed, door and window as simple boxes, seen from above.
Make a key: a small picture for each thing.
Hide a toy, mark it with an X, and let someone find it with your map.

check.question: A map is usually drawn as if you are looking...
check.explain: Maps show a bird's-eye view.

check.question: What does a map key tell you?
check.explain: The key explains each symbol on the map.

items.subject: economics
items.title: Needs, wants and swaps
items.summary: Some things we need. Some things we just want. People swap and trade to get them.
steps: List 5 things your family buys.
Sort them: needs (food, water, home) and wants (toys, treats).
Play a swap game: trade a drawing for a snack with someone at home.
Talk about it: why do people use money instead of swapping?

check.question: Which is a need?
check.explain: We need water to live. A toy is a want.

check.question: Why is money useful?
options: It is easier than finding someone to swap with
check.explain: Money lets you trade with anyone, not just someone who wants your thing.

items.subject: mathematics
items.title: Fractions with recipes
items.summary: Halve or double a simple no-cook recipe using fractions.
steps: Wash your hands and choose a no-cook recipe, like oat and fruit pots.
Read the amounts: for example 1 cup oats, 1/2 cup milk, 1/4 cup raisins.
Work out half of each amount. Half of 1/2 is 1/4. Half of 1/4 is 1/8.
Work out double each amount for a bigger family.
Measure your half or double version with cups or spoons and make it.
Check: does it taste the same? It should, because the fractions stayed in the same proportion.

safety.notes: This version uses no knives and no heat. Wash hands first and check allergies with an adult before choosing ingredients. If the recipe needs cutting or cooking, an adult does that part.

basic.description: Practise scaling with a cup and spoon using dry oats or rice, then pour it back.

better.description: Make a half batch and a double batch of a no-cook recipe and compare.

advanced.description: Convert cups to grams, scale the recipe for 3 people (1.5 times) and write the new recipe card.

substitutions.use: The same mug for every ingredient, plus a tablespoon
Use the weight printed on the packet and divide the packet into equal parts

check.question: Half of 1/2 cup is...
check.explain: Split a half into two equal parts and each is a quarter.

check.question: Double 3/4 cup is...
Why does the half batch taste the same?
options: Every ingredient was halved, so the proportions stayed the same
check.explain: Scaling every amount by the same fraction keeps the recipe in balance.

items.adultNote: Tutor tip from the brief: connect fractions to recipes for children who love cooking. Let the child do all the maths before measuring.

items.subject: biology
items.title: Heart, lungs and your pulse
items.summary: Find your pulse, then see how exercise changes your heart and breathing.
steps: Sit still. Find your pulse on your wrist below the thumb with two fingers.
Count the beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. That is beats per minute.
Count your breaths in one minute.
Do 30 seconds of gentle star jumps or marching.
Count pulse and breaths again. What changed? Why?
Learn: the heart pumps blood carrying oxygen from the lungs to your muscles.

safety.notes: Exercise gently on a non-slip floor with space around you. Stop if you feel dizzy, unwell or have pain, and tell an adult. Learners with a heart or breathing condition should follow their own doctor's advice.

materials: A clock or counting aloud in seconds
basic.description: Count pulse and breaths before and after marching on the spot.

better.description: Record pulse every minute after exercise until it returns to resting and draw a line graph.

advanced.description: Listen to the heartbeat with a funnel-and-tube stethoscope and compare results across family members.

substitutions.use: Count "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two" for seconds, or use any phone clock

check.question: After exercise your pulse usually...
check.explain: Muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster.

check.question: You count 20 beats in 15 seconds. Beats per minute?
check.explain: 20 x 4 = 80 beats per minute.

check.question: Which organ takes oxygen into the blood?
check.explain: The lungs pass oxygen into the blood; the heart pumps it around.

items.subject: physics
items.title: Friction ramp race
items.summary: Roll a toy car down a ramp onto different surfaces. Which surface stops it fastest?
steps: Make a ramp with a board or a big book propped on other books.
Roll a toy car from the same spot each time.
Measure how far it travels on a smooth floor, a towel and a rug.
Keep everything else the same: same car, same start, same ramp height. That makes it a fair test.
Record results in a table and say which surface has the most friction.

hazards: Ramp or books falling on toes
safety.notes: Build the ramp low and steady on the floor. Keep the area clear so nobody trips.

materials: Any rolling toy, bottle or can
basic.description: Compare two surfaces and measure distance in foot-lengths.

better.description: Test four surfaces, repeat each three times and average the results.

advanced.description: Change ramp angle as a second experiment and graph angle against distance.

substitutions.use: A round can, bottle or ball
Foot-lengths or string marked every 10 cm

check.question: Which surface usually has the most friction?
check.explain: Rough, bumpy surfaces grip more and slow things down.

check.question: In a fair test you change...
check.explain: Change one thing so you know what caused the result.

items.adultNote: Link to bicycles: brakes and tyres use friction. Ask why bike tyres have tread.

items.subject: geography
items.title: World map and compass
items.summary: Find the continents and oceans and use north, south, east and west.
steps: Look at a world map or globe. Find the seven continents.
Find the five oceans.
Find your country. Which continent is it on?
Use compass directions: which country is north of yours? Which is west?
Use the scale bar to estimate the distance to a country you want to visit.

check.question: How many continents are there?
check.explain: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Europe, North America and South America.

check.question: On most maps, north is at the...
check.explain: Most maps put north at the top, with a compass rose to show it.

check.question: What does the scale bar help you do?
check.explain: A scale shows how map distance matches real distance.

items.adultNote: A free printable map or an atlas from the library is enough.

items.subject: history
items.title: Build a timeline
items.summary: Make a timeline of your family or your town to see how things change over time.
steps: Ask an older relative about three things that happened when they were young.
Draw a long line and mark years along it at equal gaps.
Add your birth year, theirs and the events.
Add two big world events from the same years.
Talk about it: what was different then? What stayed the same?

check.question: On a timeline, older events go...
check.explain: Timelines run in order, from earlier to later.

check.question: A memory from a person who was there is a...
check.explain: First-hand accounts are primary sources, though memories can still be mistaken.

items.subject: writing
items.title: Write a strong paragraph
items.summary: One main idea, three details, one closing sentence.
steps: Pick a topic you know, like your favourite animal.
Write a topic sentence with the main idea.
Add three sentences with facts or examples.
Finish with a closing sentence that sums up.
Read it aloud. Does every sentence belong?

check.question: The topic sentence tells...
check.explain: It tells the reader what the paragraph is about.

check.question: A sentence about breakfast in a paragraph about elephants should be...
check.explain: Every sentence should support the main idea.

items.subject: biology
items.title: From cells to organs
items.summary: Living things are built in levels: cells make tissues, tissues make organs, organs make systems.
steps: Learn the levels: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
Compare a plant cell and an animal cell: nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria; plants also have a cell wall and chloroplasts.
Pick one organ, like the stomach, and list the tissues in it (muscle, lining, nerves).
Draw a ladder diagram from cell to you.
Explain to someone at home why a cut heals: cells divide to replace damaged ones.

check.question: Which comes first in size order, smallest to largest?
check.explain: Cells group into tissues, which form organs.

check.question: Which part do plant cells have but animal cells do not?
check.explain: Plant cells have a stiff cell wall and chloroplasts.

check.question: Where is most genetic information kept in a cell?
check.explain: The nucleus holds DNA.

items.subject: biology
items.title: Genes and inherited traits
items.summary: Why do children look a bit like their parents but not exactly the same?
steps: Learn: DNA is a code; a gene is a section of DNA that helps build a trait.
You get one copy of each gene from each biological parent.
Draw a Punnett square for a simple trait with one dominant (B) and one recessive (b) version.
Work out the chances of each combination: BB, Bb, bb.
Discuss: most real traits, like height, depend on many genes and on environment too.

check.question: Bb x Bb: what fraction of offspring are expected to be bb?
check.explain: The four boxes are BB, Bb, Bb, bb, so 1 in 4.

check.question: Height depends on...
check.explain: Most traits are polygenic and also shaped by nutrition and health.

items.adultNote: Be sensitive with adopted, foster or donor-conceived children: use animals or plants as examples, and say "biological parents".

items.subject: mathematics
items.title: Balance and solve equations
items.summary: An equation is like a balance. Do the same to both sides to find the unknown.
steps: Picture a balance: 3 bags of sweets plus 2 loose sweets weigh the same as 14 sweets. Each bag holds x.
Write it: 3x + 2 = 14.
Take 2 from both sides: 3x = 12.
Divide both sides by 3: x = 4.
Check: 3 x 4 + 2 = 14. Correct!
Now try: 5x - 3 = 22 and 2(x + 4) = 18.

check.question: Solve 5x - 3 = 22.
check.explain: Add 3: 5x = 25. Divide by 5: x = 5.

check.question: Solve 2(x + 4) = 18.
check.explain: Divide by 2: x + 4 = 9, so x = 5.

check.question: Why do we do the same thing to both sides?
check.explain: Both sides must stay equal, just like a balanced scale.

items.subject: chemistry
items.title: Red cabbage acid test
items.summary: Make a colour-changing indicator from red cabbage and test kitchen liquids.
steps: With an adult, chop some red cabbage and cover it with hot (not boiling) water. Leave 15 minutes.
Strain the purple liquid into a jug. This is your indicator.
Pour a little into several clear cups.
Add lemon juice to one, vinegar to another, baking soda in water to a third, and plain water to a fourth.
Record the colours: red/pink means acid, purple means neutral, green/blue means base (alkali).
Write a short lab report: question, method, results table, conclusion.

safety.notes: An adult handles the knife and hot water. Use only food-cupboard liquids from the steps: never test bleach, drain cleaner or other household chemicals, and never mix them. Wear glasses or sunglasses for splashes, rinse eyes with clean water if splashed, and do not drink the results.

materials: Red cabbage leaves or red onion skins
basic.description: Make the indicator and test three liquids.

better.description: Test six food-cupboard liquids and order them on a pH colour scale.

advanced.description: Compare your cabbage colours with pH paper and calibrate your own colour chart.

substitutions.use: Red onion skins, beetroot water or dark berry juice
Washed clear plastic bottles cut down by an adult, or white saucers

sources.title: Education resources for chemistry teachers and learners
Home safety
sources.publisher: Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA)

check.question: The indicator turns pink in lemon juice. Lemon juice is...
check.explain: Pink or red means acid.

check.question: Which liquid should you NEVER test at home?
check.explain: Cleaning chemicals can burn skin and make dangerous gases if mixed.

check.question: Plain water is the control. Why include it?
options: To compare the other colours with neutral
check.explain: A control shows what "no change" looks like.

items.subject: economics
items.title: Supply and demand at the market
items.summary: Why are strawberries cheaper in summer? Learn how supply and demand set prices.
steps: Pick a food that changes price through the year in your area.
Learn: supply is how much sellers offer; demand is how much buyers want.
Draw a simple graph: price up the side, quantity along the bottom. Demand slopes down, supply slopes up.
Mark where they cross: that is the market price.
Shift the supply line right for a big harvest. What happens to price?

check.question: A huge harvest means supply rises. Price usually...
check.explain: More supply with the same demand pushes price down.

check.question: A demand curve usually slopes...
check.explain: People usually buy more when the price is lower.

items.subject: history
items.title: Primary and secondary sources
items.summary: Historians are detectives. Learn to tell first-hand evidence from later accounts and question both.
steps: Learn: a primary source is from the time (a letter, photo, diary); a secondary source is written later about it (a textbook).
Find one of each about the same event, for example from a library or a museum's free website.
Ask of each: who made it, when, why, and for whom?
List what each source can and cannot tell you.
Write two sentences: what you think happened and how sure you are.

check.question: A diary written by a soldier during a war is a...
check.explain: It was made at the time by someone who was there.

check.question: Why ask who made a source and why?
options: Because purpose can shape what is included
check.explain: Every source has a point of view. Knowing it helps you judge reliability.

items.subject: biology
items.title: Homeostasis: how your body keeps balance
items.summary: Your body constantly corrects temperature, water and blood sugar using feedback loops.
steps: Learn the parts of a negative feedback loop: stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response.
Apply it to temperature: too hot leads to sweating and widening skin blood vessels; too cold leads to shivering.
Apply it to blood glucose: the pancreas releases insulin to lower it and glucagon to raise it.
Draw both loops as diagrams.
Explain in a paragraph why fever is a change in the body's set point, not a failure of control.

check.question: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
check.explain: Insulin helps cells take up glucose from the blood.

check.question: Shivering when cold is an example of...
check.explain: Muscles (effectors) shiver to generate heat.

check.question: Negative feedback works to...
options: return a value towards its set point
check.explain: It reverses the change, keeping conditions stable.

items.adultNote: Educational only: this lesson does not diagnose. Any questions about personal health go to a doctor.

items.subject: biology
items.title: Epidemiology and public health
items.summary: How do scientists track disease in whole populations, and how do communities reduce spread?
steps: Learn key terms: incidence, prevalence, outbreak, epidemic, pandemic.
Learn R, the reproduction number: how many people one case infects on average.
Model it on paper: start with 1 case and R = 2, then R = 0.8. Count cases over 5 generations.
List public health measures: clean water, sanitation, vaccination, hand washing, ventilation.
Read one WHO or national public health page and summarise how it presents data.

sources.title: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

check.question: If R is below 1, an outbreak will usually...
check.explain: Each case infects fewer than one other person on average.

check.question: R = 2. One case (generation 0) infects 2 people (generation 1). How many new cases in generation 4?
check.explain: Generations 0 to 4: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. The cases double each generation.

check.question: Prevalence means...
options: how many people have a condition at a time
check.explain: Incidence counts new cases; prevalence counts all current cases.

items.subject: biology
items.title: Nutrition science and food labels
items.summary: Understand nutrients, energy and how to read a food label with evidence, not hype.
steps: Learn the macronutrients (carbohydrate, protein, fat) and key micronutrients (vitamins, minerals), plus fibre and water.
Read the label on two packaged foods. Compare sugar, salt, fat and fibre per 100 g.
Learn why we compare per 100 g, not per serving.
Read the WHO healthy diet fact sheet and list three evidence-based recommendations.
Spot a claim in an advert and decide what evidence would be needed to support it.

check.question: Why compare foods per 100 g?
options: It is always the whole packet
check.explain: Per 100 g gives a fair comparison.

check.question: Which nutrient is the main building material for muscles?
check.explain: Proteins provide amino acids for building and repairing tissue.

items.adultNote: Keep the focus on evidence and food, not body weight or dieting. Young people with questions about their own diet should talk to a doctor or registered dietitian.

items.subject: mathematics
items.title: Functions, graphs and change
items.summary: Model real situations with linear and quadratic functions and read their graphs.
steps: A phone plan costs 5 plus 2 per gigabyte: write C = 2g + 5 and plot it.
Identify gradient (rate of change) and intercept (starting value).
A ball thrown up has height h = 20t - 5t^2. Plot t = 0 to 4.
Find when it lands and its highest point from the graph, then check by algebra.
Explain in words what the gradient means in each real situation.

check.question: In C = 2g + 5, what does 5 represent?
check.explain: It is the intercept: the cost when g = 0.

check.question: When does h = 20t - 5t^2 hit the ground (h = 0, t > 0)?
check.explain: 5t(4 - t) = 0, so t = 4 seconds.

check.question: The highest point of that ball is at t = ?
check.explain: The parabola is symmetric, halfway between 0 and 4. h = 20 metres.

items.subject: writing
items.title: Write an argument essay
items.summary: Plan, draft and revise a structured essay that takes a clear position and handles the other side fairly.
steps: Choose a debatable question, for example "Should school start later?"
Research both sides and note evidence with where it came from.
Write a thesis: your position in one sentence.
Plan: introduction, three body paragraphs (point, evidence, explanation), a counter-argument paragraph, conclusion.
Draft, then leave it a day.
Revise for clarity, cut repetition, check every claim has evidence, and list your sources.

hazards: Long screen time if researching online
safety.notes: Take breaks from screens. Research can be done from library books or printed articles.

basic.description: Hand-write the essay using two library sources.

better.description: Type the essay, use headings while drafting, and ask someone to comment.

advanced.description: Use at least one peer-reviewed or official statistic source and cite in a consistent style.

substitutions.use: Paper drafts with a different colour pen for revisions

check.question: A thesis statement is...
options: your main position in one sentence
check.explain: Everything in the essay supports or tests it.

check.question: Why include a counter-argument?
options: It shows fairness and makes your case stronger
check.explain: Answering the best opposing point builds trust with the reader.

items.subject: physics
items.title: Calculate household electricity use
items.summary: Use power and time to work out how much energy your home uses and what it costs.
steps: Find the power rating (watts) printed on three appliances. Do not open or unplug anything to look; ask an adult.
Learn: energy (kWh) = power (kW) x time (hours). 1000 W = 1 kW.
Estimate hours of use per day for each appliance.
Calculate daily and monthly kWh for each.
Multiply by your local price per kWh (from a bill) to find the cost.
Suggest two changes that would cut use, and calculate the saving.

check.question: A 2000 W heater runs for 3 hours. Energy used?
check.explain: 2 kW x 3 h = 6 kWh.

check.question: A 10 W light runs 5 hours a day for 30 days. Energy?
Where should you find the power rating?
options: On the label, or by asking an adult
check.explain: Never open electrical appliances. The label or manual has the rating.

items.adultNote: This is a calculation lesson; the child reads labels and bills only. A recent bill gives the local price per kWh.
